what_its_for: Enfuvirtide is an HIV medicine that helps control your HIV infection. It works by blocking HIV from entering your body's immune cells, which helps lower the amount of HIV in your blood and keeps your immune system stronger. It does not cure HIV, but it helps you stay healthier and reduces your risk of getting HIV-related illnesses.
how_to_take: Enfuvirtide is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection), not into a vein or muscle. You or a caregiver will inject it twice a day. Rotate your injection sites each time — use the upper arm, stomach area, or front of the thigh. Avoid injecting into moles, scars, bruises, or areas that are tender or red. Always follow the instructions your nurse or doctor gave you for mixing and injecting this medicine. Use a new needle and syringe for every injection and dispose of used needles safely in a sharps container.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 90 mg (1 mL) injected under the skin twice a day — once in the morning and once in the evening, about 12 hours apart. For children aged 6 to 16 years, the dose is based on body weight and is determined by your doctor. Always take it exactly as prescribed and do not skip doses.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still several hours before your next scheduled dose. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. Skipping doses can make your HIV treatment less effective and may cause the virus to become resistant to the medicine.
storage: Store unmixed vials of enfuvirtide powder at room temperature between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep them in the original package away from light and moisture. After you mix (reconstitute) the powder with the provided water, you must store the mixed solution in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C) and use it within 24 hours. Take the refrigerated mixed solution out 30 to 45 minutes before injecting so it warms to room temperature. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not freeze.
what_to_avoid: Do not skip doses, as this can make the medicine stop working. Avoid injecting into the same spot repeatedly — always rotate injection sites to reduce skin irritation. Do not share needles, syringes, or vials with anyone else, as this can spread HIV or other infections. Avoid touching or rubbing the injection site right after injecting. Continue to use safer sex practices (such as condoms) and do not share drug needles with others, as enfuvirtide does not prevent the spread of HIV to other people.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you notice signs of a severe allergic reaction such as rash, fever, nausea, vomiting, chills, low blood pressure, or trouble breathing. Call your doctor if you develop signs of pneumonia such as cough, fever, or difficulty breathing, as enfuvirtide may increase your risk of lung infection. Also contact your doctor if you notice signs of infection at the injection site such as increasing redness, swelling, warmth, oozing, or a hard lump that does not go away. Tell your doctor about any new or unusual symptoms while on this medicine.
when_it_works: Enfuvirtide starts working right away to block HIV from entering your cells, but it may take several weeks to months before you see changes in your blood test results (such as your viral load going down and your CD4 count going up). It is important to keep taking your medicine every day even if you feel well, because HIV is still active in your body even when you have no symptoms.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Your doctor will help weigh the benefits and risks of using this medicine during pregnancy. Children: Enfuvirtide can be used in children aged 6 years and older, with the dose adjusted based on body weight. Kidney or liver problems: Dose adjustments are generally not needed for mild to moderate kidney or liver issues, but always tell your doctor about your full medical history so they can monitor you closely. Elderly patients: Use with caution — older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, and your doctor will monitor you carefully.
